passage: Tomas walked off the pitch with his shoulders dropped and his eyes on the grass. His team had lost the final, one goal to nothing. His coach, Mateo, jogged after him. “Cheer up, it's only a game!” Tomas shrugged and kept walking. Mateo slowed down, then sat next to him on the bench. “That save you made in the second half was a tough one. I know you worked so hard.” Tomas's shoulders eased a little and he leaned against the bench. “I wanted to win,” he said, quietly.

qa.q: What was the score in the final?
qa.a: His team lost the final, one goal to nothing.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling as he walked off with his shoulders dropped, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Sadness and disappointment about the loss, since he kept his eyes on the grass. He may also have been tired after the match.

qa.q: What worked better from Mateo, telling him to cheer up or sitting beside him?
qa.a: Sitting beside him and naming his effort worked better, because Tomas's shoulders eased and he said he wanted to win. “Cheer up” made him shrug and walk on.

qa.q: How might Mateo have felt about the loss?
qa.a: Probably disappointed too, and worried about Tomas. His first “Cheer up” may have been an awkward try to help.

grounding: A child drops the shoulders after a loss; a warm word helps more than telling him to cheer up.

passage: In the hostel common room, Sunaina held her maths paper face down on her knees, her shoulders rounded like a shell. Nandini, on the next chair, saw the number on the top corner before Sunaina covered it. It was lower than either of them had expected. “Cheer up,” said another girl, passing by. Sunaina pulled her knees up. Nandini said nothing for a minute, then moved her chair closer. “That was a hard paper. I got stuck on the last question too.” Sunaina let out a breath. “I studied so much.”

qa.q: Where was Sunaina sitting with her maths paper?
qa.a: She was in the hostel common room.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling with her shoulders rounded and the paper face down, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Sadness and disappointment about the mark, and maybe embarrassment, since she covered it and pulled her knees up. She may also have been tired from studying.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that helped, unlike the girl who said “Cheer up”?
qa.a: She stayed quietly close and shared that she too got stuck, which let Sunaina say how she felt. The other girl's words brushed the feeling aside.

qa.q: How might Nandini be feeling herself?
qa.a: She may be a bit disappointed and worried for her friend too, since she got stuck on the last question as well.

grounding: A child drops the shoulders after disappointing marks; a warm word helps more than cheer up.

passage: I'm Chandrika, from the flat opposite, and I was watering my tulsi when Farhan came up the stairs after the badminton final. His racket hung from one hand. His shoulders had sunk so low his school bag slid off one side, and he didn't hitch it back. His mother opened the door. “Cheer up, beta, it's only a game!” she said brightly. Farhan's shoulders dropped even more. His grandfather, behind her, said nothing at first. He just took the bag and said, “Three sets in that heat. Tiring, and disappointing.” Farhan leaned into him. I don't know what he felt, but his shoulders came up a little.

qa.q: How many sets did Farhan play?
qa.a: Farhan played three sets in the heat.

qa.q: What do Farhan's sinking shoulders suggest after the final?
qa.a: They suggest he felt sad and defeated after losing, too low even to hitch his bag back up.

qa.q: Why did the grandfather's words help more than “Cheer up”?
qa.a: He named the effort and the disappointment warmly, so Farhan felt understood instead of told to hide his feeling.

qa.q: How does Chandrika read Farhan's mood?
qa.a: Chandrika only sees the sunk shoulders and the lean into his grandfather, and doesn't claim to know his feelings.

grounding: Shows a child's dropped shoulders after a loss, and a warm word helping more than being told to cheer up.

passage: Monday: Pooja walked out of the school gate holding her maths test, 38 out of 50, and her shoulders slumped so low her bag straps slipped. Her brother Chinmay, waiting on his cycle, said, “Oh, stop sulking. Chin up!” Pooja's shoulders sank further, and she walked home without a word. Wednesday: Chinmay knocked on her door. “Sorry about Monday. I got a worse mark in Class 6. You studied every night; I saw. It's okay to feel rubbish about it.” Pooja's shoulders loosened. Saturday: Pooja brought her fractions book to Chinmay's desk. “Will you check these?” She sat up straight while he did.

qa.q: What mark did Pooja get on her maths test?
qa.a: Pooja got 38 out of 50.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when her shoulders slumped at the gate?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and defeated by the mark, after studying every night.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change on Wednesday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He apologised, shared his own worse mark and said it was okay to feel rubbish, which gave warmth instead of an order to cheer up.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Chinmay?
qa.a: Chinmay may have meant to help, but his quick “Chin up” made his sister feel worse, which he realised later.

grounding: Shows a child's dropped shoulders after disappointing marks, and a warm word helping more than telling her to cheer up.

passage: Karthik, you asked why I still keep that old bronze medal. Listen, then. I, your Aparna Athai, was eleven and sure I'd win the district race. I came third. When I walked off the track, my shoulders fell so low I felt shorter. My father met me at the gate and said, “Enough long face. Smile, people are watching.” I tried, and it felt like swallowing a stone. Then my coach, Mrs Pillai, sat beside me on the bench. She didn't tell me to smile. She said, “You wanted gold badly, and you ran your hardest. It's allowed to hurt.” I cried on her shoulder. The next year, I ran again.

qa.q: Where did young Aparna come in the district race?
qa.a: Aparna came third.

qa.q: What was young Aparna feeling as she walked off the track?
qa.a: She felt deeply disappointed and defeated, her shoulders falling so low she felt shorter.

qa.q: What choice did Mrs Pillai make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She didn't ask for a smile but named Aparna's effort and hurt, which let her cry and later run again.

qa.q: How might Aparna's father have felt about his words?
qa.a: He probably wanted to protect her pride in front of others, not realising that asking for a smile made her feel worse.

grounding: Shows a child's dropped shoulders after a loss, and a warm word helping far more than being told to smile.

passage:
Rain had turned the district track to mud by the time the girls' 400 metres started. Uma slipped on the last bend, went down on one knee, got up and finished last. At the line her shoulders dropped, her arms hung and she stared at her spikes.

"Cheer up, it's just one race!" called a teammate from under the tarpaulin. Uma's shoulders sank lower.

The bus was leaving in five minutes, and Coach Zubin was herding thirty wet children with one umbrella. Still, he stopped beside her. "That one hurt. You fell, got up and finished in that mud. I saw it."

Uma didn't smile, but she walked to the bus beside him, shoulders a little higher.

qa.q: Where did Uma slip?
qa.a: On the last bend.

qa.q: What do Uma's dropped shoulders and her stare at her spikes suggest?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and defeated after falling and finishing last; she may also have felt embarrassed in front of her team.

qa.q: Why did Coach Zubin's words help more than "Cheer up"?
qa.a: He named how it felt and noticed the effort of getting up and finishing, which respected her sadness instead of brushing it off.

qa.q: What is it like for Coach Zubin to stop for Uma just then?
qa.a: Coach Zubin is rushed, with a bus leaving and thirty wet children, so stopping is a real choice to put one upset runner first.

grounding: It shows a child's dropped shoulders after losing a race, and a warm word from a coach helping more than being told to cheer up.
